note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · PALE FLATTENED ANNUAL CROWN
tiles.details: Bob Harms's source-identified dried uprooted specimen (panel 10) shows true fibrous roots and attached flattened culms, while Harry Rose's in-situ photo (panel 1) shows field growth but hides the root crown. Goosegrass is an annual bunchgrass with notably compressed pale/whitish basal sheaths in life, NOT a network of rooting perennial runners. Neither photograph proves the LIVE milky-white crown at diagnostic close range. Next photograph: fresh uprooted living crown, fibrous roots, emerging tillers and cm scale.
tiles.short: LOOK HERE FIRST: pale compressed tiller bases radiating from one tough fibrous-rooted center
tiles.status: DRIED ROOTED WHOLE PLANT AND IN-SITU HABIT PHOTO; PALE LIVING CROWN MACRO STILL NEEDED

tiles.heading: 02 · SHORT NOTCHED MEMBRANOUS LIGULE
tiles.details: Look at Harry Rose's independently CC BY 2.0 licensed photographed INNER blade–sheath junction (panel 2): it shows a pale joining rim and longer side hairs. Bob Harms's photograph (panel 4) adds another actual collar-area view. Penn State describes a small centrally divided jagged MEMBRANOUS ligule typically 1–1.5 mm; Harry Rose describes ~0.5–1 mm. No existing photo provides a physical millimeter ruler for the free membrane. The two arrows identify the collar search region and separate lateral hairs only, NOT certified membrane length.
tiles.short: Open the blade–sheath junction: ~0.3–1 mm short membrane, sometimes ciliate or split
tiles.status: TRUE COLLAR PHOTO PLUS TWO GROSS ARROWS; MEMBRANE EDGE NOT CALIBRATED

tiles.heading: 03 · TWO ZIPPER ROWS ON FLAT FINGERS
tiles.details: Bob Harms's actual complete attached head (panel 9) and raceme macro (panel 8) show the stout fingerlike branches with neatly paired ranks of nearly awnless flattened spikelets; the original NC-SA flowering photo is panel 0 and remains license-conditional. Head architecture is photographed, but not continuously linked to one locally collected living crown. An additional head-only picture is not a priority.
tiles.short: Several stiff digitate or subdigitate branches carry two neat ranks of tightly appressed spikelets
tiles.status: COMPLETE ATTACHED FLOWERING HEAD AND ZIPPER ROWS PHOTOGRAPHED

tiles.heading: 04 · MULTIFLORED 4–7 MM SPIKELET
tiles.details: Harry Rose's real, source-PREANNOTATED multi-flowered spikelet (panel 3) identifies lower and upper GLUMES plus at least two separately labelled LEMMA/PALEA pairs; Bob Harms's source macro (panel 5) provides another reproductive view. Flora descriptions give roughly 3–9 florets per flattened spikelet, but these particular pictures lack physical mm scales. A single spikelet is NOT the full fingerlike branch. Distinguish author annotations from a new validated calibrated dissection.
tiles.short: One flattened spikelet contains about 3–9 florets, not just one or two
tiles.status: REAL SOURCE-ANNOTATED GLUMES/LEMMAS VISIBLE; 1-MM VOUCHER DISSECTION MISSING

tiles.heading: 05 · TWO SHORT GLUMES, AWNLESS LEMMAS
tiles.details: Photographed actual source labels on panel 3 show two glumes, lemmas and paleas; see panel 5 for reproductive context. Goosegrass fertile lemmas are generally awnless and keeled, with multiple florets in one spikelet. Never claim lengths or count invisible units directly from these photographs; a ruler and separated mature floret series remain necessary for certification.
tiles.short: Lower glume ~1.5–2.5 mm; upper ~2–4.5 mm; fertile lemmas ~2.5–5 mm (NZ flora)
tiles.status: REAL SOURCE-ANNOTATED GLUMES/LEMMAS VISIBLE; LENGTHS NOT PHOTO-MEASURED

tiles.heading: 06 · CHECK CRABGRASS, BERMUDA AND CHLORIS
tiles.details: Compare actual OTHER-species panel 11 (Digitaria ciliaris), panel 12 (Cynodon dactylon stolon), and panel 13 (Chloris virgata feathery awned head) with goosegrass panel 2 (short membranous collar). Bermudagrass roots at runner nodes and has a hair-fringe ligule; Chloris can have long bristly awns; Digitaria differs in small/floret arrangement. Identify by BASE + COLLAR + SPIKELET together, not a fingerhead alone.
tiles.short: Count florets, inspect the ligule and follow runners before deciding from a fingerhead
tiles.status: FIELD COMPARISON — MATCHED LOCAL SPECIMENS/PHOTO QA PENDING

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: GOOSEGRASS (INTRODUCED): go BASE → COLLAR → HEAD. (1) Annual fibrous-rooted rosette of very FLATTENED pale or silvery-white basal tillers; outward shoots come from one crown and do NOT form rooting stolons/rhizomes. (2) Young blades are FOLDED, not rolled; at the leaf-sheath junction examine a SHORT jagged, sometimes centrally notched MEMBRANOUS ligule (~0.2–1.5 mm depending on source), with hairs nearby but NOT a ligule made only of hairs. (3) A seedhead has several stiff FINGERLIKE branches, often one lower branch; each flat branch bears TWO neat zipperlike rows of flat AWNLESS spikelets. Mature spikelets about 3–7 mm and usually 3–9 fertile florets EACH; count florets inside ONE spikelet, not the seeds or branches. Only an original seedhead image was locally installed before this pass; new licensed Commons parts photographs are EXTERNAL references.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Flattened tillers radiate outward from a central, often whitish/silvery crown; stems may become ascending when unmowed. Mature plant is tough and often conspicuous in compacted turf or disturbed soil.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Leaves are folded in the bud (vernation), with a pronounced keel/crease. Blade bases and collar may bear sparse long hairs; do not confuse those hairs with the ligule itself.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Harry Rose's real, source-PREANNOTATED multi-flowered spikelet (panel 3) identifies lower and upper GLUMES plus at least two separately labelled LEMMA/PALEA pairs; Bob Harms's source macro (panel 5) provides another reproductive view. Flora descriptions give roughly 3–9 florets per flattened spikelet, but these particular pictures lack physical mm scales. A single spikelet is NOT the full fingerlike branch. Distinguish author annotations from a new validated calibrated dissection.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

panels.label: Actual blade–sheath collar — short membrane area and longer side hairs
panels.caption: Harry Rose's source-identified true collar photo shows a pale inner blade–sheath joining zone and much longer side hairs. The inner short membranous ligule itself is not fully resolved against a physical millimeter scale. Do not label long lateral hairs as a hair-only ligule.

panels.caption: Original photographer's pre-annotated actual multi-flowered spikelet: glumes, two lemmas and paleas named in source pixels. No ruler; species-level exact organ dimensions not verified. This photo already EXISTS in the species' local images folder.
panels.creator: Harry Rose (Macleay Grass Man)

panels.label: 6 · BERMUDAGRASS LOOK-ALIKE — actual aboveground runner
panels.caption: This is BERMUDAGRASS, not goosegrass. This real horizontal stolon carries multiple leaf-producing nodes along a creeping perennial shoot; some roots may need a better-focused node macro, so do not label any unclear roots in this photograph. Goosegrass spreads from one flattened annual crown, without a perennial stolon network.
panels.creator: no rights reserved
panels.modifications: Resized from original, reencoded JPEG and EXIF stripped; original unchanged; no arrows on this first gallery install
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: 7 · FEATHER FINGERGRASS LOOK-ALIKE — feathery awned branches
panels.caption: This is FEATHER FINGERGRASS, not goosegrass. Its radiating or gathered branches look plumose and bristly from lemma awns/hairs, whereas goosegrass has fairly regular, stout, toothlike AWNLESS spikelet rows in a zipper pattern. This gross photo cannot measure exact awn length of any one fertile lemma.
panels.creator: Matt Lavin
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

memory_rule: G = GOOSEGRASS: FLAT WHITE CROWN → FOLDED new LEAF → tiny notched MEMBRANE → flat zipper spikelet ROWS → 3–9 FLORETS in ONE spikelet. Cynodon has true rooted runners and a HAIR ligule; Chloris has bristly AWNED florets.
